resources.string: This app shows typical accessibility barriers in mobile apps and how to avoid them. Try the examples with a screen reader to experience the difference.

The contrast ratio is often overlooked when developing mobile apps. Yet a good contrast ratio matters to everyone, especially on mobile devices, for example when using them outdoors in bright sunlight. Below are some examples of good and bad contrast ratios.
Passed with a contrast ratio of __?, HEX: #ffffff on #006400.
Failed with a contrast ratio of __?, HEX: #ffffff on #bb86fc.
Passed with 21.0:1, HEX: # f f f f f f on #000000.
Failed with 2.3:1, HEX: # f f f f f f on #a0b0a1.
Just failed with 4.4:1, HEX: # f f f f f f on #0083a1.
Passed with a contrast ratio of __?, HEX: # f f f f f f on #006400.
Failed with a contrast ratio of __?, HEX: # f f f f f f on #bb86fc.
The following examples show what TalkBack reads aloud in the three most common situations: no alternative text, decorative graphics, and informative graphics.
In this example, the alternative text was intentionally omitted. In practice, alternative text is very often omitted by mistake.
This graphic is purely decorative, so its alternative text was left empty. TalkBack therefore ignores the graphic and does not read out unnecessary text.
In this example, the graphic is informative, so it was given an alternative text.
The following example shows how TalkBack behaves when a visible label is not linked to its input field.
In the first input field, the link to the visible label was intentionally omitted. The second input field is correctly linked to its label.
Tap the button below to show the full name.
Please enter a first or last name and tap the corresponding Send button.
This example shows how TalkBack behaves with image buttons that have no alternative text. It also shows how buttons can be made easier to use for people with limited fine motor skills.

On the first image button, the alternative text was intentionally omitted and the touch target was not adjusted. The second image button, in contrast, is labeled correctly and has an enlarged touch target, which makes it easier to tap.
Question 1: What is the current version of WCAG?
Answer 1: The current version of WCAG is 2.2.
Question 2: When was the current version of WCAG released?
Answer 2: The current version was released in October 2023.

People with limited fine motor skills may not be able to use a touch screen. It is therefore important that an app can also be operated with a Bluetooth keyboard and that the focus order of its controls is correct.
In the first example, the focus order was intentionally ignored. In the second example, it is correct.
Oops, something is wrong with the focus order.
Now the focus order is correct.

People with motor impairments may find it difficult or impossible to use a touch screen and therefore use a Bluetooth keyboard. This requires, among other things, that the keyboard focus is clearly visible.

In this example, the visibility of the keyboard focus was intentionally ignored for some buttons. Connect a Bluetooth keyboard to your mobile device and try to find and activate button 3 without counting how many times you press the Tab key.
This example shows how TalkBack behaves when checkboxes have not been implemented correctly.
The first set of checkboxes was implemented without taking accessibility into account. The second set was implemented with accessibility in mind.
Question 1: Do you know how to program?
Question 2: Do you plan to learn programming?
Yes, I am planning to learn programming.
No, I am not planning to learn programming.
That is fine too. There are plenty of other things you can do.
Good, programming is an exciting hobby.
Perhaps you will become interested in programming later on.
The app processes data only locally and does not send it to other devices or to third-party services. The data is also not stored permanently.
The app contains two sample forms. The data you enter in these forms is processed only locally and displayed on this device.
